interviewBank.q: What happens between the source file and a running program?
interviewBank.answer: Preprocessing expands includes and macros, compilation translates each translation unit to an object file, the linker resolves symbols against libraries, and the loader maps the executable into memory before `main` runs. A missing function definition fails at link time, not compile time.

interviewBank.q: Why does `main` return an int?
interviewBank.answer: The return value is the process exit status: 0 means success and a non-zero value reports failure to the shell and to whatever script launched the program. `return 0;` at the end of main is implicit, but writing it makes the intent explicit.

interviewBank.q: Why is C++ compiled instead of interpreted, and what does that buy the program?
interviewBank.answer: The compiler translates the whole translation unit to machine code ahead of time, so type errors surface before the program runs and execution needs no interpreter in the loop. That is why a C++ binary starts fast and has predictable performance.

interviewBank.q: What does `#include <iostream>` actually do?
interviewBank.answer: It asks the preprocessor to copy the contents of the iostream header into the translation unit, which declares `std::cout`, `std::cin` and the stream operators. It does not link anything by itself; the linker brings in the standard library implementation.

defenseBank.q: A new learner asks why their code does not run after saving the file. What do you check first?
defenseBank.answer: Saving is not compiling. I check whether a compiler was actually invoked and whether the binary they ran is the one just built.
steps: Confirm the compile command and its exit status.
Confirm the path of the binary that was executed.
Read the first compiler error, not the last.

defenseBank.q: Why teach `std::cout` instead of `using namespace std;`?
defenseBank.answer: The `std::` prefix keeps every name visible at its use site and avoids the collisions that a global using-directive invites. For a beginner the extra five characters are cheaper than a name clash they cannot diagnose.

modules.title: Program Structure and Input/Output
modules.goal: Read the parts of a C++ program and take typed input from the user without leaving the stream broken.

topics.title: Reading input with cin
topics.body: `std::cin >> x` skips whitespace and reads one value into `x`. Reading into a string stops at the first space, which is why full names need `getline`.

topics.title: getline reads the whole line
topics.body: `std::getline(std::cin, line)` keeps spaces. Mixing `>>` and `getline` leaves a newline in the buffer, so consume it first.

topics.title: Formatting output
topics.body: `std::fixed` and `std::setprecision` come from `<iomanip>` and control decimals; the setting persists until you change it.

topics.title: Escape sequences you will actually use
topics.body: `\t` inserts a tab, `\n` ends the line, `\\` prints a backslash and `\"` prints a quote. Each sequence is one character in the string even though it is typed as two.

topics.title: Reading fields from a string stream
topics.body: `std::istringstream` behaves like `std::cin` but reads from a string, which makes parsing testable without waiting for a keyboard. `>>` splits on whitespace and converts to the requested type.

interviewBank.q: Why does `cin >> name` lose the second word of a full name?
interviewBank.answer: Formatted extraction treats whitespace as a delimiter: it reads until the next space and leaves the rest in the buffer. `getline` reads to the newline instead, which is the correct tool for a line of text.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `\n` and `std::endl`?
interviewBank.answer: Both write a newline, but `std::endl` also flushes the stream. Flushing every line is unnecessary in most code and costs performance in loops, so `\n` is the default choice.

interviewBank.q: Why does `std::cin >> name` stop at the first space?
interviewBank.answer: The extraction operator treats whitespace as the field separator, so it reads one token. A full line needs `std::getline`, and mixing the two requires clearing the leftover newline first.

interviewBank.q: Why does `std::setw` affect only the next output field?
interviewBank.answer: Width is consumed by the single insertion that follows it, while flags such as `std::left`, `std::fixed` and the fill character persist. That is why an aligned table repeats `setw` per column but sets the alignment once.

defenseBank.q: A menu program loops forever after a bad input. Explain the cause.
defenseBank.answer: When extraction fails, `cin` sets its failbit and leaves the bad characters in the buffer, so the next read fails immediately. The fix is to detect failure, clear the state and ignore the rest of the line.
steps: Check `if (!std::cin)` after every read.
Call `std::cin.clear()` and `std::cin.ignore(...)`.
Re-prompt instead of proceeding with an unsent value.

defenseBank.q: Why is input validation part of the lesson, not an advanced extra?
defenseBank.answer: A program that trusts its input is a program that corrupts its own state on the first typo. Validation is cheaper to teach at the point of input than to debug later as a mysterious loop.

interviewBank.q: Why is `double` the default for decimals instead of `float`?
interviewBank.answer: `double` has roughly twice the precision and is the type of unsuffixed floating literals, so it avoids the silent rounding that `float` introduces in ordinary calculations. `float` is for storage-sensitive cases, not the default.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between initialization and assignment?
interviewBank.answer: Initialization gives a variable its first value as it is created; assignment replaces a value that already exists. A `const` can be initialized but never assigned, which is why the distinction matters to the compiler.

interviewBank.q: When should a value be `const` instead of `constexpr`?
interviewBank.answer: `const` promises the value will not change after initialization but may be computed at runtime; `constexpr` requires it to be computable at compile time. Use `constexpr` when the value must participate in compile-time checks or array bounds.

interviewBank.q: Why does `unsigned` subtraction wrap instead of going negative?
interviewBank.answer: Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo two to the power of the type width, so subtracting past zero wraps to a huge positive value. That is well-defined, not undefined, and it is exactly why counts that can go negative should be signed.

defenseBank.q: Why is an uninitialized local variable dangerous even when the program seems to run?
defenseBank.answer: Its value is indeterminate, so reading it is undefined behaviour: the output can change between builds, compilers and optimisation levels. A test that passes today proves nothing about it.

defenseBank.answer: When it hides a conversion or an ownership decision the reader needs to see. `auto x = 1.5;` is fine; `auto p = makeWidget();` is only fine if the widget type is obvious from the name.

modules.title: Operators and Type Conversion
modules.goal: Use arithmetic, comparison, logical and bitwise operators without falling into integer division or implicit-conversion traps.

topics.title: Integer division and modulus
topics.body: Two ints divide as integers and discard the remainder. Convert one side to `double` when you need the fractional part; `%` gives the remainder.

topics.title: Comparison and logic
topics.body: Comparisons produce bools, `&&` and `||` combine them with short-circuit evaluation, and `!` negates. A chained comparison like `1 < x < 3` does not mean what it looks like.

topics.title: Bitwise operators
topics.body: `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<` and `>>` work on the bits of an integer. They are used for flags and masks, and they are not the same as the logical operators.

topics.title: Integer division and modulus together
topics.body: `/` between two ints truncates toward zero and `%` returns the remainder with the sign of the left operand. The two results always satisfy `a == (a / b) * b + a % b`.

topics.title: Prefix and postfix increment differ
topics.body: `a++` yields the old value and then increments, while `++a` increments and yields the new value. Reading both in one expression is where beginners lose track of the order.

interviewBank.q: Why does `7 / 2` print 3 and not 3.5?
interviewBank.answer: Both operands are ints, so the division is integer division and the fractional part is discarded. Making one operand a double, for example `7 / 2.0`, selects floating-point division.

interviewBank.q: When is `static_cast` preferable to a C-style cast?
interviewBank.answer: `static_cast` states which conversion is intended and is checked at compile time for incompatible types, so a reviewer can see it. A C-style cast can silently become a reinterpret_cast, which is much harder to justify.

interviewBank.q: What is operator precedence and why does it matter?
interviewBank.answer: Precedence decides which operator binds first when several appear without parentheses; `*` before `+`, for example. When the intent is not obvious, parentheses are cheaper than a reader re-deriving the table.

interviewBank.q: Why is `static_cast<double>(a) / b` safer than relying on implicit conversion?
interviewBank.answer: It states the conversion at the exact point it matters, so the division is floating point even if both operands are ints. Implicit conversion can happen later than the author expects, leaving integer division in place.

defenseBank.q: A learner writes `int avg = total / count;` and the average is wrong. What do you ask?
defenseBank.answer: I ask for the types of total and count before touching the formula: if both are integers, the division already lost the fraction before the assignment.

Check for a divide-by-zero path.
Convert one operand and re-test with a case that has a remainder.

defenseBank.q: Why are implicit conversions a common source of bugs?
defenseBank.answer: They are invisible at the call site, so a `double` narrowing to `int` or a negative `int` converting to `unsigned` reads like a normal assignment. Braces and explicit casts make the conversion visible.

topics.title: The for loop
topics.body: A `for` loop names its counter, its bound and its step in one line, which makes the number of iterations readable at a glance.

topics.title: while and a sentinel

topics.title: Range-based for

topics.title: do-while runs once before checking

interviewBank.q: When is a do-while the right loop?
interviewBank.answer: When the body must run at least once, such as showing a menu or reading a value before validating it. The condition is checked after the body, so the first pass is unconditional.

interviewBank.q: Why is `continue` sometimes a readability problem?
interviewBank.answer: It skips the rest of the body, so a reader has to hold every earlier continue in mind to know what actually executes. A guard clause or an if-else is often clearer.

interviewBank.q: When would you choose `while` over `for`?
interviewBank.answer: `for` when the iteration count or the counter is the point of the loop, `while` when the loop ends on a condition that is not a counter, such as reading until end of input.

interviewBank.q: Why does a range-based for not need an index?
interviewBank.answer: It iterates with `begin()` and `end()`, so the container supplies the bounds. That removes the off-by-one class of bug and works for containers that have no index at all.

topics.title: Declare, define, call
topics.body: A declaration tells the compiler a function's signature; the definition supplies the body. The call site only needs the declaration, which is why headers work.

topics.title: Pass by reference
topics.body: A reference parameter aliases the caller's object, so the function can change it without pointers. `const&` avoids the copy but forbids the change.

topics.title: Recursion needs a base case
topics.body: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input and stops at a base case. Without the base case the call stack grows until it overflows.

topics.title: Default arguments fill the gap
topics.body: A default argument is used only when the caller omits that argument; it is written once in the declaration. Defaults must be trailing, so a parameter with a default cannot precede one without.

topics.title: Passing by reference changes the caller
topics.body: A reference parameter is another name for the caller’s object, so writing through it mutates the original. Passing by value would modify only the copy and leave the caller unchanged.

interviewBank.q: Why is `std::string` preferred over `char[]`?
interviewBank.answer: It owns and resizes its buffer, knows its length, supports value semantics and cannot silently overflow the way a fixed array can. A `char[]` remains useful only at API boundaries or for fixed binary data.

interviewBank.q: What does `npos` mean?
interviewBank.answer: It is the constant returned by `find` when nothing matched. Because it is the largest possible position value, comparing against it is the correct test instead of comparing with -1.

interviewBank.q: Why does `std::array` not decay when passed to a function?
interviewBank.answer: It is a class object, not a raw array, so passing it by value copies the whole array and passing by reference keeps its type and length. That is why the size is still available inside the callee.

interviewBank.q: When is `std::vector` the better choice than `std::array`?
interviewBank.answer: When the element count is decided at runtime or must grow. `std::array` is for a fixed compile-time size and avoids a heap allocation entirely.

modules.title: Pointers and References
modules.goal: Understand addresses, dereference safely, and choose between a pointer, a reference and a value.

topics.title: Address and dereference
topics.body: `&x` yields the address of x, and `*p` reads the value stored there. A pointer is a variable whose value is an address.

topics.title: A reference is an alias
topics.body: A reference must be bound when created and cannot be rebound. Writing through it writes to the original, which is why swap takes references.

topics.title: Pointers walk an array
topics.body: Array elements are contiguous, so `p + 1` moves to the next element. The one-past-the-end pointer is valid for comparison but must never be dereferenced.

topics.title: split a string with find and substr
topics.body: `find` returns the position of a character or `std::string::npos`, and `substr(pos, len)` copies a slice. Combining them splits a record without a regular expression.

topics.title: string_view is a non-owning window
topics.body: `std::string_view` stores a pointer and a length, so taking a substring or passing it to a function copies no characters. It is valid only while the underlying string is alive.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a pointer and a reference?
interviewBank.answer: A pointer is an object that stores an address, can be null, can be rebound and needs dereferencing. A reference is an alias bound once, cannot be null and is used with ordinary syntax. Prefer a reference when the argument must exist.

interviewBank.q: Why is dereferencing a dangling pointer undefined behaviour?
interviewBank.answer: The object it points to has ended, so the memory may be reused or unmapped. Reading or writing there has no defined result, and the program can appear to work until the allocator reuses that block.

interviewBank.q: What does `std::string::npos` mean?
interviewBank.answer: It is the value returned by `find` when nothing matched, defined as the largest representable size type. Comparing against it is the check, not comparing against `-1` by hand.

interviewBank.q: When is `std::string_view` unsafe?

interviewBank.q: What does RAII guarantee?
interviewBank.answer: That a resource is released when its owning object's lifetime ends, including during stack unwinding from an exception. The destructor is the release point, so no manual cleanup path can be forgotten.

interviewBank.q: When would you choose shared_ptr over unique_ptr?
interviewBank.answer: Only when several independent owners must keep the same object alive and no single owner can define its lifetime. Exclusive ownership is simpler and cheaper, so unique_ptr is the default.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a pointer and a reference?
interviewBank.answer: A pointer is an object that stores an address and can be null or reassigned; a reference is an alias that must be bound and cannot be reseated. References have no null state, which removes one class of bug when the target is required.

interviewBank.q: What makes a pointer dangle?
interviewBank.answer: The object it points at is destroyed or freed while the pointer still holds the old address. Reading or writing through it is undefined, so lifetime has to outlive every pointer to it.

defenseBank.q: How do you find a memory leak in a small program?
defenseBank.answer: I look for every new and check for a matching delete on all paths, then run the program under AddressSanitizer, which reports the allocation that leaked.
steps: List allocation sites and their release paths.
Check early returns and exception paths.
Rebuild with -fsanitize=address and read the report.

defenseBank.q: Why is `delete p; delete p;` worse than a leak?
defenseBank.answer: A leak wastes memory but leaves the program defined. A double delete corrupts the allocator's bookkeeping, which is undefined behaviour and often crashes somewhere unrelated later.

interviewBank.answer: The only language difference is the default access: public for a struct, private for a class, and public for inheritance from a struct. Convention uses struct for passive data and class for types with invariants.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer enum class to a plain enum?
interviewBank.answer: It is scoped, so enumerator names cannot collide, and it is strongly typed, so no implicit conversion to int. A plain enum leaks its names into the enclosing scope and converts silently.

interviewBank.q: What does RAII mean in practice?
interviewBank.answer: A resource is acquired by an object’s constructor and released by its destructor, so scope and the type system guarantee cleanup. It works for memory, files, locks and sockets alike.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer `make_shared` to `shared_ptr<T>(new T)`?
interviewBank.answer: It allocates the object and the control block in one allocation, which is faster and exception-safe. The raw `new` form can leak if an exception occurs between allocation and the smart pointer construction.

interviewBank.q: Inheritance or composition: how do you decide?
interviewBank.answer: If the derived type genuinely is a kind of the base and must be usable through its interface, inheritance fits. If it merely uses the other type's behaviour, composition is safer and does not couple the two hierarchies.

interviewBank.q: What is the diamond problem?
interviewBank.answer: Two base classes sharing a common ancestor give the most-derived object two copies of that ancestor, so a member reference is ambiguous. Virtual inheritance solves it by sharing one base subobject, at a cost in complexity.

interviewBank.q: What is the Rule of Three?
interviewBank.answer: If a class needs a custom destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, it usually needs all three because they manage the same resource. Modern code often reaches for the Rule of Zero instead by holding a smart pointer.

interviewBank.q: Why is `explicit` used on single-argument constructors?
interviewBank.answer: It blocks implicit conversions from the argument type, so a function taking the class cannot silently accept a raw value. The conversion must be written at the call site.

defenseBank.q: Why can deep inheritance hierarchies become fragile?
defenseBank.answer: A change in a base class reaches every derived class, and the derived classes may depend on protected details that were never a contract. Composition keeps that dependency explicit and local.
steps: Count how many classes depend on the base's details.

defenseBank.q: What does the base constructor run before the derived one?
defenseBank.answer: Construction goes base first so the derived body can rely on a fully constructed base. Destruction goes the other way: derived first, then base.

topics.title: virtual enables dynamic dispatch
topics.body: A virtual function is chosen by the object's dynamic type, not the pointer's static type. `override` makes a signature mismatch a compile error instead of a silent new function.

topics.title: Object slicing loses the derived part
topics.body: Copying a derived object into a base value slices off the derived fields, so the virtual call uses the base version. Pass by reference or pointer instead.

topics.title: Construction runs base before derived
topics.body: A derived object contains its base subobject, so the base constructor completes first and the derived body runs after. Destruction is the exact reverse: derived first, then base.

interviewBank.q: Why does a polymorphic base need a virtual destructor?
interviewBank.answer: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer runs only the base destructor when it is not virtual, so the derived part is never destroyed. That is undefined behaviour and typically leaks.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?
interviewBank.answer: Overloading picks a function by argument types at compile time within one scope. Overriding replaces a virtual function in a derived class and is selected at runtime by the object's type.

interviewBank.q: What does the diamond problem describe?
interviewBank.answer: Two paths to the same base class create two base subobjects, so members are ambiguous and state is duplicated. Virtual inheritance collapses them into one shared base, at the cost of a more complex object layout.

interviewBank.q: Why is composition often preferred to inheritance?
interviewBank.answer: It couples to behaviour rather than to a type hierarchy, so the contained class can be swapped and tested independently. Inheritance is for a genuine IS-A relationship and a stable base interface.

defenseBank.answer: When the type is known at compile time or the hot path cannot afford an indirect call. Templates or plain overloads resolve earlier and inline better.

interviewBank.q: What is template instantiation?
interviewBank.answer: It is the compiler generating a concrete function or class for the types actually used. Nothing is generated for types you never instantiate, which is why template errors often appear at the call site.

interviewBank.q: Why do template errors look so long?
interviewBank.answer: The compiler reports the full instantiation chain from your call down into the library. The useful line is usually the first note that names your type and the requirement that failed.

interviewBank.q: Which operators cannot be overloaded?
interviewBank.answer: `::`, `.`, `.*`, `?:` and `sizeof`. Everything else that takes at least one class-type operand can be overloaded, though doing so should preserve the operator’s expected meaning.

interviewBank.q: Why is `operator=` usually a member function?
interviewBank.answer: It needs access to the object being assigned and must return `*this` by reference for chaining. The compiler-generated copy assignment is a member for the same reason.

defenseBank.q: When is a template unnecessary?
defenseBank.answer: When only one type is ever used, or when the abstraction forces every caller into the same algorithm. A plain function or a small interface is easier to read and debug.
steps: Count the real instantiations.
Check whether the types share the required operations.
Prefer the simpler non-template version when they do not.

defenseBank.q: What does it mean that templates are header-only in practice?
defenseBank.answer: The compiler needs the full definition to instantiate, so the body usually lives in the header. Putting it in a .cpp leaves other translation units unable to generate the code.

interviewBank.q: vector, list or deque: how do you choose?
interviewBank.answer: Default to vector for contiguous storage and cache locality. Use deque when you need fast insertion at both ends, and list only when stable iterators and frequent middle insertion outweigh the pointer overhead.

interviewBank.q: map or unordered_map?
interviewBank.answer: map when order matters or you need range queries, unordered_map when average constant lookup matters more and the key can be hashed. The unordered version trades ordering and worst-case guarantees for speed.

interviewBank.q: Why must a template usually be defined in a header?
interviewBank.answer: The compiler needs the definition to instantiate it for each type at the point of use. A definition hidden in a .cpp file is invisible to other translation units, producing link errors.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a template and a macro?
interviewBank.answer: A template is type-checked, scoped and instantiated by the compiler. A macro is textual substitution with no type safety, which is why templates replaced most macro-based generic code.

defenseBank.q: Why does `map::operator[]` sometimes create a bug?
defenseBank.answer: It inserts a default-constructed value for a missing key, so a lookup that was meant to be read-only silently grows the container and changes later results.

modules.title: Iterators, Algorithms and Lambdas
modules.goal: Replace hand-written loops with algorithms, pass behaviour as a lambda, and understand iterator invalidation.

topics.title: Algorithms take iterator ranges
topics.body: `std::sort` receives a begin and an end iterator, so it works on any contiguous or random-access range. Half-open ranges mean the end is one past the last element.

topics.title: A lambda is a local function object
topics.body: `[](int x) { return x > 2; }` is an anonymous callable. Captures bring in local state; `[&]` captures by reference and `[=]` by value.

topics.title: accumulate folds a range
topics.body: `std::accumulate` combines the elements with an initial value. The initial value's type is the result type, so `0.0` is needed for a double mean.

topics.title: map keeps its keys sorted
topics.body: `std::map` orders keys by `operator<`, so iteration is sorted without an extra sort. Lookup is logarithmic and the container stores one value per unique key.

topics.title: unordered_map counts without promising order
topics.body: The hashed container gives average constant-time lookup, which is why it is the usual choice for frequency tables. Iteration order is unspecified, so never print it as if it were sorted.

interviewBank.q: Why is erase(remove(...)) a two-step operation?
interviewBank.answer: remove_if moves the kept elements forward and returns the new logical end, but it cannot change the container's size because it only sees iterators. erase then removes the tail, which is why both calls are required.

interviewBank.q: What invalidates a vector iterator?
interviewBank.answer: Any reallocation, and any insertion or erase at or before the iterator's position. Reallocation happens on growth, so a stored iterator can dangle after a push_back even if no element was erased.

interviewBank.q: How do you choose between `map` and `unordered_map`?
interviewBank.answer: Choose `map` when ordered iteration or range queries matter, and `unordered_map` when lookup speed is the priority and order is irrelevant. The hashed version needs a hash function and can degrade under bad hashing.

interviewBank.q: What is iterator invalidation?
interviewBank.answer: An operation that reallocates or restructures the container leaves existing iterators pointing at freed or moved storage. A vector push_back may invalidate all iterators, while a node-based map only invalidates the erased element’s iterator.

defenseBank.q: When is a hand-written loop clearer than an algorithm?
defenseBank.answer: When the loop performs several different actions in one pass, or the algorithm would need a lambda so complex that the loop is shorter. Algorithms win when they name a single operation.

Keep the loop when the body does more than one thing.

defenseBank.q: Why do lambdas capture by reference carefully?
defenseBank.answer: A reference capture keeps a pointer to a local that may be gone when the lambda is called later, which is a dangling reference. Capture by value when the lambda outlives the scope.

modules.title: Exception Handling and Error Management
modules.goal: Signal failure with exceptions, catch them at the right level, and keep objects consistent while unwinding.

topics.title: throw, try, catch
topics.body: `throw` transfers control to the nearest matching `catch`. Stack objects are destroyed on the way out, which is what makes RAII the partner of exceptions.

topics.title: A custom exception type
topics.body: Derive from `std::runtime_error` when callers may want to catch a category. The `what()` message should say what failed, not just that something failed.

topics.title: noexcept is a promise
topics.body: `noexcept` states that a function will not throw. If it does, the program terminates, so mark only operations that genuinely cannot fail or must not.

topics.title: sort with a lambda comparator
topics.body: The third argument is any callable that answers "does a come before b?". A lambda keeps the rule next to the call, and the sort stays stable only if `stable_sort` is used.

topics.title: accumulate needs the right seed type
topics.body: The initial value fixes the accumulator’s type. Seeding with `0` keeps integer arithmetic even when the range holds doubles, while `0.0` makes the average a real division.

interviewBank.q: Why check is_open instead of assuming the file exists?
interviewBank.answer: Opening can fail for permissions, a missing directory or a locked file, and a failed stream stays in a failed state. Reading it yields nothing, so the program continues with empty data unless the open is checked.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a text and a binary stream?
interviewBank.answer: A text stream may translate line endings, while a binary stream reads and writes the bytes exactly. Use binary for serialized structures, images or anything whose bytes must round-trip unchanged.

interviewBank.q: What does `noexcept` promise?

interviewBank.q: When should an exception not be used?
interviewBank.answer: For expected, frequent conditions such as "not found" where a return value or `std::optional` is clearer and cheaper. Exceptions are for exceptional failure that the immediate caller cannot handle.

modules.title: Modern C++ and Version Evolution
modules.goal: Use the features that changed everyday C++: auto, nullptr, range-for, optional, structured bindings and constexpr.

topics.title: auto and nullptr
topics.body: `auto` deduces from the initializer; `nullptr` is a typed null pointer constant, unlike `NULL` which is an integer. Overload resolution can tell them apart.

topics.title: Range-for and structured bindings
topics.body: `for (const auto& [key, value] : map)` names both halves of a pair without `first` and `second`, which makes loops over maps readable.

topics.title: optional models absence
topics.body: `std::optional<T>` either holds a value or holds nothing, which is clearer than a sentinel. Check it before use; `value()` throws when empty.

topics.title: A file stream closes at the end of its scope
topics.body: The `ofstream` destructor flushes and closes the file, so a nested scope is enough to make the write visible. Reading afterwards then sees the complete contents.

topics.title: filesystem splits a path
topics.body: `std::filesystem::path` understands separators, so `filename()` and `extension()` work on any platform instead of being hand-parsed from a string.

interviewBank.q: Why is nullptr better than NULL?
interviewBank.answer: `nullptr` has its own type, so it converts to any pointer type without becoming an integer. `NULL` is usually 0, which can select an int overload and hide a bug.

interviewBank.q: When should a function return optional instead of a pointer?
interviewBank.answer: When absence is a normal outcome and the value is small or cheap to move. A pointer suggests an object already exists somewhere; optional suggests the function may produce one or none.

interviewBank.q: Why check a stream after opening it?
interviewBank.answer: A failed open leaves the stream in a failed state and every extraction returns immediately, so the program silently works with empty data. `is_open()` or a boolean test turns that into an explicit error path.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between text and binary mode?
interviewBank.answer: Text mode may translate line endings on some platforms, while binary mode reads the exact bytes. Structured records should be read and written in binary with fixed layouts.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between O(n log n) and O(n)?

interviewBank.q: What does `if constexpr` solve?
interviewBank.answer: It discards the untaken branch during instantiation, so a template can use operations that are valid for some types but not others. A plain `if` still has to compile both branches.

interviewBank.answer: Two threads access the same memory, at least one writes, and there is no synchronisation ordering them. In C++ that is undefined behaviour, not just an unexpected value.

interviewBank.q: Why is a mutex not a complete concurrency design?
interviewBank.answer: It keeps one critical section correct but introduces contention and deadlock risk, and it does not make a compound operation across several calls atomic. The design has to define the invariant and which lock owns it.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between assert and an exception?
interviewBank.answer: An assertion documents an internal precondition that should never be false and is removed in release builds. An exception reports a runtime failure that callers are expected to handle, such as invalid input.

interviewBank.q: Why compile with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic?
interviewBank.answer: They surface uninitialised reads, unused results, narrowing conversions and non-standard extensions before they become runtime bugs. A warning-clean build is cheaper than finding the same defect in production.

interviewBank.q: What is a data race?
interviewBank.answer: Two threads access the same memory concurrently, at least one writes, and no synchronization orders them. The result is undefined behaviour, not merely an unpredictable value.

interviewBank.q: What does a mutex actually protect?
interviewBank.answer: It protects the invariant that the locked region is supposed to maintain, not the variable by itself. Every access to the shared state must take the same lock or the protocol is broken.

defenseBank.q: How do you structure a small C++ project?

steps: Separate declarations from definitions.

Put the executable's entry point in its own file.

defenseBank.q: What does the One Definition Rule forbid?
defenseBank.answer: Two different definitions of the same function or object in one program. Declarations can repeat, definitions cannot, which is why headers hold declarations and source files hold bodies.

interviewBank.q: How do you present a project in a 5-minute interview?
interviewBank.answer: Problem, constraints, the one design decision that mattered, the result with a number, and one thing you would change. The rest belongs in the repository README.

interviewBank.q: When is a design pattern unnecessary complexity?
interviewBank.answer: When there is only one implementation and no sign of a second: a factory for one type or an observer with one listener adds indirection without a decision to make. Patterns pay for variation.

interviewBank.q: What does the Rule of Five add to the Rule of Three?
interviewBank.answer: Move construction and move assignment, so a resource can be transferred instead of copied. A class that declares one of the five should consider all five.

interviewBank.q: Why is `const` correctness a design tool rather than decoration?
interviewBank.answer: It encodes which operations may mutate state, so the compiler rejects accidental writes and the interface documents itself. It also enables passing by const reference without losing the ability to call readers.

defenseBank.q: Why is Singleton criticised despite being common?

practice.task: A class that owns its members through RAII types needs no destructor, copy constructor or assignment operator; the compiler-generated ones are correct. That is less code and fewer chances to get lifetime wrong.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: A move-only class

defense.q: Why is Singleton criticised despite being common?
defense.answer: It is global state with a constructor, so tests cannot substitute it and dependencies are hidden. A passed-in object with an interface gives the same single instance without the coupling.
steps: Name the hidden dependency.

defense.q: What makes a C++ portfolio project credible?
defense.answer: It builds with one documented command, has tests for the core rules, handles bad input and explains its trade-offs. A small finished project beats a large half-written one.
